newsitem.title: USA: Milwaukee Brewers win approval for new ballpark.
newsitem.headline: Milwaukee Brewers win approval for new ballpark.

text.p: The Southeast Wisconsin Professional Baseball Park District Board gave the go-ahead Monday to begin immediate site preparation work for a new $250-million, partly-bond financed stadium for the Milwaukee Brewers American League Baseball Team.
However, the board will not give final approval for the issuance of $160-million of tax-exempt bonds until its November meeting, according to Robert Trunzo, the board's chairman.
Once that approval is in hand, Pat Born, a senior vice president at Evenson Dodge, the board's financial advisor, said the deal would be priced and closed by year-end.

He and officials from Bear Stearns and Co. Inc., the senior manager on the deal, told the board it was necessary to sell the bonds as soon as possible in order to avoid running into any retroactive effective date in U.S. Senator Patrick Moynihan's bill to end the use of tax exempt bonds for professional sports stadiums.
That bill is expected to be re-introduced early next year but with a new effective date to replace the previous June 14, 1996 date.

However, the actual sale of the bonds could be delayed past year-end, according to Born. He said he and underwriters would recommend the board not sell any bonds until a lawsuit challenging the legality of a 0.1 percent, five-county sales tax, to back the bonds, is resolved.
Born said he has received indications from legal counsel that the Federal court judge hearing the case should decide on a motion to dismiss it by year-end.

The convertible-roofed stadium would be financed with the proceeds from the bond as well as $50-million in loans to the Brewers from the City of Milwaukee, the city's local business community and two foundations. The remaining $40 million would be raised through the sale of naming rights to Miller Brewing Company, upfront concession payments, and a $10-million letter of credit from the American Baseball League.

In June, concerns over cost over-runs and the inability of the Brewers to raise some of its $90-million share of the financing led the board to kill the project. However, Trunzo said he was confident the project can be brought in at $250-million dollars.
